v.why: Pushing an already large L2 penalty toward 1 underfits badly, so raising alpha hurts much more when alpha is already high.
Extra weight decay stabilises Adam at large learning rates, so adding alpha helps more when the learning rate is high.
Raising an already large learning rate causes divergence, so the effect is much more negative in the high band.
With tiny learning rates the model is undertrained in 243 epochs, so increasing the rate helps most there.
Small batches give noisy gradients, so a larger learning rate is more likely to destabilise training.
Larger batches reduce gradient noise and effective step size, which rescues unstable high-learning-rate training.
With a tiny learning rate, bigger batches mean fewer updates and more underfitting.
Deeper networks are more prone to divergence under large learning rates.
When learning is slow, extra depth adds capacity and gradient pathways that improve the underfit model.
Narrow networks are capacity-limited, so adding width helps most when width is small.

raw:
I based these on patterns in the 100 measurements and on known MLP/Adam behaviour. Only one seed was run per experiment, so these are best guesses, not confirmed effects.

- **Learning rate is the strongest modifier.**
  - At high learning rates (0.0774 and up), raising it further collapsed accuracy (#52, #56).
  - At high learning rates, adding alpha (#9), batch size (#29, #32) or width (#71) stabilised training and helped.
  - At very low learning rates, raising it helped (#54).
  - Adding depth was harmful at high learning rates (#88, #95) and helpful at low ones (#87, #99).
- **Large alpha is harmful.** Raising alpha from 0.129 to 1 consistently cost 3–16 points.
- **Small batches make a high learning rate worse.** With batch size 4, a higher learning rate collapsed accuracy (#52).
- **Large batches with tiny learning rates cut the number of updates.** Raising the batch size here reduced accuracy (#33).
- **Narrow networks gain the most from more width.** This shows in #62, #73 and #77.
